cards.explanation: The answer is the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth. Paul says he is an apostle “…for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness…” (Titus 1:1). That's the purpose he names right in his opening line. I wish my old resume had been that tidy.

The answer is that He cannot lie. Paul says the promise of eternal life came from “…God, who cannot lie…” (Titus 1:2). The One who made the promise is the One who cannot lie. A promise from someone like that is one you can count on.

The answer is True. Paul says God promised eternal life “…before time began.” (Titus 1:2). That's older than any recipe I've ever baked, and older than the oven too. Before the clock even started, the promise was already made.
The answer is God our Savior. Paul says the proclamation was entrusted to him “…by the command of God our Savior.” (Titus 1:3). The command came from God. That's the source Paul names.
The answer is elders. Paul says Titus was to “…appoint elders in every town…” (Titus 1:5). Every town, friends, no skipping. That's a lot of towns and a lot of appointing.
The answer is False. Paul says an elder must be blameless, “…the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers…” (Titus 1:6). His home gets named in the requirements. It counts.

The answer is that they should be believers. Paul says the elder has “…children who are believers…” (Titus 1:6). Then he adds that they must not be open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination. His household gets looked at, not just him.

The answer is False. Paul says an overseer must be above reproach, and “not quick-tempered” is on the list of what he must not be (Titus 1:7). Being above reproach in other ways doesn't cancel it out.

The answer is True. Paul says, “Instead, he must be hospitable…” (Titus 1:8). After a long list of what not to be, he turns to what an overseer must be. Hospitable means making room for people, and my bakery is always open for that.

The answer is to encourage others and refute those who contradict it. Paul says the overseer holds firmly to the faithful word “…so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.” (Titus 1:9). The word is for building people up and for answering those who push against it.

The answer is silenced. Paul says of those full of empty talk and deception that they “…must be silenced.” (Titus 1:11). He goes on to say that for the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not. That's the situation Titus is facing.

The answer is dishonorable gain. Paul says, “For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households…” (Titus 1:11). So they're after something for themselves, and whole households pay for it. That's a steep price for someone else's profit.
The answer is True. After quoting the prophet, Paul says, “This testimony is true.” (Titus 1:13). He's leaning on the quote to make his point. And then he gives Titus what to do about it.
The answer is to rebuke them sternly. Paul says, “Therefore rebuke them sternly…” (Titus 1:13). Sternly is the word he chooses. He adds the reason too, which is that they will be sound in the faith.

The answer is so they will be sound in the faith. Paul says to rebuke them sternly “…so that they will be sound in the faith” (Titus 1:13). The aim is for them to be sound in the faith. It's a hard word with a hopeful goal behind it.

The two answers are myths and truth. Paul wants them to “…pay no attention to Jewish myths…” (Titus 1:14). Not a little attention, friends, none. He also says not to pay attention to “…the commands of men who have rejected the truth.” (Titus 1:14). Those commands come from men who turned the truth down.

The answer is nothing. Paul says, “To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.” (Titus 1:15). Two very different outcomes in one sentence, and 'nothing' is the strong one.
The answer is False. Paul says, “…both their minds and their consciences are defiled.” (Titus 1:15). So the minds aren't clean either. The word 'both' covers the two of them.

The answer is that their actions deny Him. Paul says, “They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.” (Titus 1:16). Words can say one thing while a life says another. The actions give them away.

The answer is False. Paul says they are “…detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.” (Titus 1:16). He doesn't leave a few good deeds on the table for them. The verse also says they profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.
